teaser: Sondera's commander's intent and our behaviour policies are one idea: twelve terms joined, the business layer above, and five rules tested in Cedar.
core_idea: Sondera argues that agents do not go rogue but fill unstated gaps, so limits must be written as effects, compiled into checkable rules and enforced outside the agent, which is commander's intent; joined to this site's vocabulary it is the mandate, the gap and the barriers of an agent behaviour policy, with this site going further up into the business layer, where only the company can write the limits, and Sondera going further in proof by compiling plain English into Cedar; five rules from both sides and the business layer evaluated in Cedar gave fourteen of fourteen intended verdicts, and the hard part is where each rule's facts come from.

quotes.text: An agent has no intent, just an optimization target.
quotes.why: Why the limits have to be ours.

quotes.text: So limits have to be written about effects, not actions.
The rule that the user interface enforced by omission is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something enforces it.
quotes.why: Why the business layer has to be written now.

figures.caption: Two vocabularies, one idea: twelve of Sondera's terms from "Your Agents Need Commander's Intent" against the terms this site and RiskMandate use. Most are the same idea in different words; we extend theirs at the business layer, and they extend ours with proof.

Limits about effects, all the way up. Sondera's published example sits just above the mechanics; the business logic sits above it, and each layer can be written as an effect and compiled to the same kind of rule. What changes going up is where the facts come from: the platform, the session, the ledger, the CRM, and at the top, judgement.
